paragraphs: The Americans live in a democratic state of society, which has naturally suggested to them certain laws and a certain political character. This same state of society has also produced among them a multitude of feelings and opinions that were unknown among the older aristocratic communities of Europe. It has destroyed or modified all the relations that existed before and established others of a new kind. The aspect of civil society has been affected by these changes no less than that of the political world. I dealt with the political side in the work on the Democracy of America, which I published five years ago; to examine the other is the object of the present book. But the two parts complete each other and form one and the same work.

I must warn the reader at once against an error that would be extremely damaging to me. When he finds that I attribute so many different consequences to the principle of equality, he may infer that I consider that principle to be the sole cause of everything that happens in the present age. But that would be to impute to me a very narrow view. A multitude of opinions, feelings, and tendencies now exist that owe their origin to circumstances unconnected with the principle of equality, or even contrary to it. If I took the United States as an example, I could easily prove that the nature of the country, the origin of its inhabitants, the religion of its founders, their acquired knowledge, and their former habits have exercised, and still exercise, a vast influence on the thoughts and feelings of that people, independently of democracy. Different causes, no less distinct from the circumstance of equality of conditions, could be traced in Europe, and would explain a great part of what is taking place among us.

I acknowledge the existence of all these different causes and their power, but my subject does not lead me to treat them. I have not undertaken to explain the reason for all our inclinations and all our notions. My only aim is to show in what respects the principle of equality has modified both.

Some readers may perhaps be astonished that — firmly persuaded as I am that the democratic revolution we are witnessing is an irresistible fact, against which it would be neither desirable nor wise to struggle — I should so often have had occasion in this book to use language of such severity toward the democratic communities that this revolution has brought into being. My answer is simply this: it is because I am not an adversary of democracy that I have tried to speak of democracy with complete sincerity.

People will not accept truth from their enemies, and their friends seldom offer it to them. For this reason I have spoken it. I was persuaded that many would take it upon themselves to announce the new blessings that the principle of equality promises to mankind, but that few would dare to point out from afar the dangers with which it threatens them. I have therefore turned my chief attention to those perils, and believing that I had clearly discovered them, I did not have the cowardice to leave them untold.

I trust that my readers will find in this Second Part the same impartiality that seems to have been noted in the earlier work. Placed as I am amid the conflicting opinions that divide us, I have tried to suppress within myself for a time the favorable sympathies or hostile feelings that each of them inspires in me. If those who read this book can find a single sentence meant to flatter any of the great parties that have stirred my country, or any of the petty factions that now harass and weaken it, let them raise their voices to accuse me.

The subject I have tried to embrace is immense, for it includes the greater part of the feelings and opinions to which the new state of society has given birth. Such a subject is doubtless beyond my strength, and in treating it I have not satisfied myself. But if I have not been able to reach the goal I had in view, my readers will at least do me the justice of acknowledging that I conceived and pursued my undertaking in a spirit not unworthy of success.
Section I: Influence of Democracy on the Action of Intellect in the United States.
